text: And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places…
reflection: Isaiah paints a picture of home that every heart longs for: "And my people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, and in sure dwellings, and in quiet resting places." Peaceable. Sure. Quiet. These words describe more than a building. They describe a life settled in God's care. Isaiah spoke them to a nation surrounded by turmoil, promising that when God's righteous King reigned, His people would finally know security and rest. Many of us live in noisy, hurried, uncertain places. Our homes may be busy, our minds restless, our futures unclear. But God's promise is that He Himself is our dwelling place. In Him, our souls can find a quiet resting place, even when the world outside is loud. As we begin this month of peace, rest, and renewal, ask God to make your heart a peaceable habitation. Create a small space of quiet in your day. Sit with Him. Let His presence settle you. His peace is a home you can return to anytime.
question: Where could you create a small space of quiet to sit with God today?
prayer: Lord, make my heart a peaceable habitation, a sure dwelling, and a quiet resting place. Settle me in Your presence, and let Your peace be my home. Amen.

text: Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep.
reflection: When Lazarus died, Jesus told His disciples that their friend was sleeping. They were relieved, thinking he was simply resting. John explains, "Howbeit Jesus spake of his death: but they thought that he had spoken of taking of rest in sleep." Jesus used the gentle word sleep to describe death. For those who belong to Him, death is not the end. It is like falling asleep, with the certainty of waking again. Jesus was on His way to raise Lazarus, demonstrating that He has power over the grave. This brings deep comfort to anyone who has lost a loved one in Christ. They are not lost forever. They rest in Him, and one day they will rise. It also brings peace when we think about our own mortality. We do not need to fear the end. In Jesus, even death becomes a kind of rest. Today, rest in His presence and in His promise. The One who calls death sleep is the One who will wake us.
question: How does Jesus' promise of waking change the way you think about death and loss?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You call death sleep, and You are the One who will wake us. Take away my fear of the end, and let me rest in Your promise of life. Amen.

text: And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called. And they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee.
reflection: Blind Bartimaeus sat by the road, calling out to Jesus. The crowd told him to be quiet, but he cried louder. Then everything changed: "And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called. And they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee." Jesus stood still. In the middle of a busy crowd, on His way to Jerusalem, He stopped for one man. That is the heart of our Savior. He is never too busy for you. He hears the cry others try to silence. And the message to Bartimaeus is the message to you: be of good comfort, rise, He is calling you. Resting in God's presence begins with knowing that He has stopped for you. He sees you, hears you, and calls you near. Today, if you feel overlooked or lost in the crowd, take comfort. Jesus has stood still for you. Rise, and come to Him. He is calling your name.
question: Where do you feel overlooked, and how does it comfort you that Jesus stands still for you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You stand still for me and call my name. When I feel lost in the crowd, help me take comfort, rise, and come to You. Amen.

text: To whom he said, This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing: yet they would not hear.
reflection: Through Isaiah, God offered His people a gift: "This is the rest wherewith ye may cause the weary to rest; and this is the refreshing." He was pointing them to the rest and refreshing found in trusting Him. But the verse ends with sad words: "yet they would not hear." They refused the very thing they needed. Instead of resting in God, they kept striving, making alliances, and trusting their own plans. It is possible to be offered rest and still refuse it. Many of us do this. God invites us to slow down, to trust Him, to lay down our burdens. Yet we keep running, worrying, and carrying everything ourselves. We say we are too busy to rest. But God's rest is not laziness. It is the deep refreshment of trusting Him. Today, do not be like those who would not hear. Listen to His invitation. Choose a moment to stop, breathe, and trust. Receive the rest and refreshing He freely offers.
question: What invitation to rest from God have you been refusing to hear?
prayer: Lord, You offer rest to the weary and refreshing to the tired. Help me hear Your invitation, stop striving, and receive the rest of trusting You. Amen.

text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
reflection: Jesus offers one of the most beautiful invitations in Scripture: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls." A yoke was a wooden frame that joined two animals so they could work together. Jesus is not promising a life without work. He is promising a life of shared work, where He carries the weight with us. And His yoke fits well. It is shaped by His gentle and humble heart. Many of us are wearing heavy yokes: the yoke of perfectionism, people-pleasing, fear, or trying to earn God's approval. These burdens wear us down. Jesus invites us to exchange them for His. When we walk with Him, learning from His gentle ways, we find rest for our souls, even in the middle of busy days. Today, identify a burden that has been weighing you down. Lay it at His feet. Take His yoke instead, and learn to walk in step with Him.
question: What burden have you been carrying that you can exchange for Jesus' yoke today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are meek and lowly in heart. I lay my heavy burden at Your feet and take Your yoke instead. Teach me to walk in step with You and find rest. Amen.

text: And he said unto her, Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.
reflection: A woman had suffered with bleeding for twelve years. She had spent everything on doctors and only grown worse. In desperation, she pushed through the crowd and touched the hem of Jesus' garment. Immediately she was healed. Then Jesus turned and spoke to her with tenderness: "Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." He called her daughter. After years of isolation, she was welcomed into a family. He commended her faith. And He sent her away with peace. Jesus did not only heal her body; He restored her dignity and calmed her heart. This is what faith in Jesus brings: wholeness. Not just physical healing, but peace and belonging. Perhaps you have been struggling for a long time. You may feel worn out and alone. Reach out to Jesus in faith, even if your faith feels small. He welcomes you, and He speaks peace over your life. Go in peace today.
question: What long struggle can you bring to Jesus in faith, even if your faith feels small?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You welcome me and speak peace over my life. I reach out to You in my long struggle. Make me whole, and let me go in Your peace. Amen.

text: Therefore we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all.
reflection: Paul had been anxious about the church in Corinth. He had written them a hard letter and worried about how they would respond. Then Titus arrived with good news, and Paul's heart lifted: "we were comforted in your comfort: yea, and exceedingly the more joyed we for the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by you all." Comfort spread from one person to another. The Corinthians refreshed Titus, Titus brought joy to Paul, and Paul's comfort flowed back to the church. This is how God often comforts the weary: through people. A kind word, a visit, a helpful hand, a shared joy. When we refresh someone else's spirit, the comfort multiplies. Is there someone who has refreshed your spirit lately? Thank God for them. And consider how you might refresh someone else today. A message of encouragement, a meal, or a listening ear can become part of a chain of comfort that reaches further than you know.
question: Whose comfort has refreshed you lately, and whom could you refresh today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the people who have refreshed my spirit. Make me part of Your chain of comfort, and help me encourage someone today. Amen.

text: Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied.
reflection: After a season of intense persecution, the early church entered a time of peace: "Then had the churches rest throughout all Judaea and Galilee and Samaria, and were edified; and walking in the fear of the Lord, and in the comfort of the Holy Ghost, were multiplied." Rest did not make them lazy. It made them stronger. They were edified, built up in faith. They walked in reverence for God and in the comfort of the Spirit. And they grew in number. Seasons of rest are gifts from God, and they have a purpose. They allow us to heal, to grow deeper roots, and to prepare for what comes next. We should not feel guilty when God gives us a season of calm. Nor should we waste it. Use it to be built up in Him. If you are in a quieter season right now, receive it gratefully. Draw near to God, let the Spirit comfort you, and let your faith grow strong. Rest is part of how God builds His people.
question: If you are in a quieter season, how can you use it to grow stronger in faith?
prayer: Lord, thank You for seasons of rest. Build me up in faith, let me walk in reverence for You and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, and let my faith grow strong. Amen.

text: And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
reflection: A furious storm struck the Sea of Galilee. Waves crashed over the boat, and the disciples were terrified. Then Jesus "arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm." Three words from Jesus, and the storm obeyed. The chaos that had threatened their lives gave way to a great calm. This is the authority of our Savior. Nature itself listens to His voice. And the same Jesus speaks into the storms of our lives today. Not every storm ends immediately. Sometimes He calms the storm; sometimes He calms us in the storm. But either way, His word brings peace. Whatever winds are howling around you, anxiety, conflict, uncertainty, grief, bring them to Jesus. Ask Him to speak His peace over your situation and over your heart. He is in the boat with you. And when He speaks, peace follows. Let Him say to your heart today: peace, be still.
question: What storm do you need Jesus to speak "Peace, be still" over today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, wind and waves obey Your voice. Speak Your peace over the storm in my life and over my anxious heart: Peace, be still. Amen.

text: And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again.
reflection: When Jesus sent out seventy disciples, He gave them instructions about bringing peace into homes: "And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again." A son of peace is someone open to God's peace, ready to receive it. The disciples were to offer peace freely. If it was welcomed, it would rest there. If not, it would return to them. Nothing would be wasted. This is a gentle and freeing principle. We are called to be people who carry God's peace into every place we go. But we are not responsible for how others receive it. Some will welcome it gladly. Others will not. Either way, the peace is not lost. It stays with us. Today, carry God's peace into your home, your workplace, and your conversations. Offer kindness and calm. Do not be discouraged if it is not always received. God's peace remains with you, and it will find hearts ready to receive it.
question: Where can you offer God's peace today, whether or not it is received?
prayer: Lord, make me a carrier of Your peace in my home, my work, and my conversations. When my peace is not received, keep it with me, and lead me to hearts ready to receive it. Amen.

text: And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.
reflection: Paul ends his letter to the Romans with a promise and a blessing: "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you." It is striking that the God of peace is the One who crushes the enemy. Peace, in God's kingdom, is not passive. It is the result of victory. Paul echoes the very first promise in Genesis, that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head. That promise was fulfilled at the cross, and its full effects are coming shortly. Every force of evil that disturbs our peace will be defeated. In the meantime, we are not left alone. The grace of Jesus is with us. If you feel under attack today, whether by temptation, discouragement, or fear, remember that the God of peace fights for you. Victory is certain. And until that day, His grace is enough to sustain you through every struggle.
question: Where are you under attack, and how does it help to know the God of peace fights for you?
prayer: God of peace, You will crush the enemy under my feet. When temptation, discouragement, or fear attacks me, remind me that victory is certain and Your grace is enough. Amen.

text: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him.
reflection: The Thessalonian believers were grieving friends and family who had died. Paul wrote to comfort them: "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him." Our hope for those who have died in Christ is rooted in the resurrection of Jesus. Because He rose, they will rise. Because He lives, they will live. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to grieve. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope. Grief is real and right, but it is held within a larger hope. Those who sleep in Jesus are safe with Him, and one day we will be reunited. Living by faith means holding on to this promise when loss makes the world feel dark. If you are missing someone today, let this verse speak comfort to your heart. Jesus died and rose again. Those who belong to Him are not lost. God will bring them with Him.
question: Whom are you missing today, and how can the hope of the resurrection comfort you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You died and rose again, and those who sleep in You are not lost. Comfort me in my grief, and fill me with hope of the day You will bring them with You. Amen.

text: But I trust in the Lord Jesus to send Timotheus shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state.
reflection: Paul was in prison, concerned for his friends in Philippi. He wanted to know how they were doing. So he wrote, "But I trust in the Lord Jesus to send Timotheus shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state." Notice the phrase I trust in the Lord Jesus. Even his travel plans were placed in God's hands. Paul did not know what the future held, but he trusted the One who did. And his desire was relational. He wanted to hear about his friends so that his heart could be comforted. There is peace in placing our plans in God's hands. We make plans, as Paul did, but we hold them loosely, trusting the character of Jesus. And there is comfort in caring for one another. Today, bring your plans to God and trust Him with them. Then reach out to someone you care about. Ask how they are really doing. Your concern may comfort them, and their news may comfort you.
question: Whom could you reach out to today to ask how they are really doing?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I trust You with my plans. Give me a caring heart for those I love, and help me reach out to someone today with genuine concern. Amen.

text: And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellow workers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me.
reflection: In his closing greetings, Paul mentions a few of his co-workers, including one called Jesus Justus. Then he says something tender: "These only are my fellow workers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me." Paul was in prison, and many had abandoned him. But these few had stayed. They worked beside him and became a comfort to his weary heart. We do not know much about these people. Their names appear only briefly in Scripture. But their faithfulness mattered deeply to Paul. They remind us that comfort often comes through ordinary, faithful friends who simply show up. You may not think of yourself as important in God's work. But your presence in someone's life can be a great comfort. Your loyalty, your encouragement, and your willingness to stay when others leave are precious to God. Today, be a comfort to someone who is weary. And thank God for those faithful few who have comforted you.
question: Who are the faithful few who have comforted you, and who needs your comfort today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the faithful people who stayed beside me and comforted me. Make me a quiet comfort to someone who is weary today. Amen.

text: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.
reflection: The psalmist had been through deep trouble, even facing death. But God had delivered him. Now he speaks to his own soul: "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee." This is a powerful practice. Sometimes we need to talk to our souls. We need to remind ourselves of truth when our emotions are anxious and unsettled. The psalmist tells his soul to return to rest. Why? Because God has been generous. He has dealt bountifully. Rest is possible because God has proven Himself good. Your soul may be restless today. Worries may circle in your mind. Speak this verse to yourself. Remind your soul of the ways God has been good to you. List His blessings. Recall His faithfulness. Then invite your soul to come home to rest. You do not have to stay in anxiety. You can return to the peace of God, because He has dealt bountifully with you.
question: What blessings can you recall today to help your soul return to rest?
prayer: Lord, You have dealt bountifully with me. When my soul is anxious, remind me of Your faithfulness, and call me home to rest in You. Amen.

text: And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?
reflection: During a terrible storm, the disciples panicked. And where was Jesus? "And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow." They woke Him and cried, "Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Jesus was not asleep because He did not care. He was asleep because He was at perfect peace. He trusted His Father completely. No storm could disturb the rest of His soul. The disciples, however, assumed that His calm meant indifference. We sometimes do the same. When God seems quiet in our storms, we wonder if He cares. But His quiet is not neglect. He is fully in control. There is a deep invitation here. Jesus shows us what it looks like to rest in God's presence, even in chaos. That kind of peace is available to us too. Today, if you feel tossed by storms, remember that Jesus is in the boat. He cares deeply. Lean on Him, and learn to rest as He rested.
question: In what storm have you wondered whether Jesus cares, and how can you rest as He rested?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You care for me even when I cannot feel it. You are in the boat with me. Teach me to rest in the Father's care as You did, even in the storm. Amen.

text: Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger.
reflection: Proverbs gives a warning that may seem surprising in a month about rest: "Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep; and an idle soul shall suffer hunger." There is a difference between rest and laziness. God's rest refreshes and renews us for faithful living. Slothfulness, on the other hand, slowly drains life away. It is a kind of spiritual drowsiness, where we drift without purpose and stop caring about what matters. And it leaves the soul hungry. This proverb helps us see that true renewal is not the same as doing nothing. Our souls are renewed not only by stillness but by meaningful engagement with God and His purposes. Rest prepares us for good work, and good work makes rest sweet. Today, examine whether you are resting or simply drifting. If you have grown spiritually sleepy, ask God to wake you up. Feed your soul with His Word. Take one purposeful step. Let rest renew you for a life that is fully awake to God.
question: Where have you grown spiritually sleepy, and what purposeful step can wake you up?
prayer: Lord, keep me from slothfulness and drift. Wake me up, feed my soul with Your Word, and let my rest renew me for a life fully awake to You. Amen.

text: But Jesus held his peace. And the high priest answered and said unto him, I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God.
reflection: Jesus stood before the high priest as false witnesses lied about Him. The accusations flew, but "Jesus held his peace." He did not defend Himself, argue, or retaliate. Then the high priest demanded, "I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God." Only then did Jesus speak, and He spoke the truth. His silence was not weakness. It was strength under control. He knew who He was. He did not need to win the argument to be secure. He was at peace because He trusted His Father with the outcome. When we are misunderstood or falsely accused, our instinct is often to defend ourselves loudly. But Jesus shows another way. There is a time for silence and a time to speak. Peace allows us to know the difference. Today, if you face criticism or misunderstanding, ask God for the peace Jesus had. You do not have to prove yourself. Rest in who God says you are.
question: When you face criticism, how can you rest in who God says you are instead of proving yourself?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You held Your peace when You were falsely accused. Give me Your peace, so I know when to be silent and when to speak, and rest in who You say I am. Amen.

text: The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: (he is Lord of all:)
reflection: Peter stood in the home of Cornelius, a Roman officer, and explained the good news: "The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: (he is Lord of all:)." This was a groundbreaking moment. Peter, a Jewish believer, was entering the home of a Gentile and declaring that the peace of Jesus was for everyone. Jesus is Lord of all. Not just of one nation, culture, or group, but of all people. The peace He brings is peace with God, and it also breaks down walls between people who were once divided. This verse reminds us that God's peace is wider than our comfort zones. It reaches people we might never expect. And it calls us to be messengers of that peace across every boundary. Today, think of someone different from you, in culture, background, or perspective. Pray for them. Show them kindness. Remember that the peace of Jesus is for them too, because He is Lord of all.
question: Who is different from you whom you can pray for and show kindness to today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are Lord of all, and Your peace is for everyone. Help me see people who are different from me as those You love, and show them kindness. Amen.

text: And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.
reflection: Paul ends his letter to the Galatians with a blessing for all who live by the gospel: "And as many as walk according to this rule, peace be on them, and mercy." The rule he means is the truth he has just stated: what matters is not outward religious markers but being a new creation in Christ. Those who walk in that truth receive peace and mercy. Peace with God and peace within. Mercy for every failure and weakness. These are gifts for the journey. And notice the word walk. The Christian life is a daily walk, step by step, in the freedom of grace. As we walk, God's peace and mercy rest upon us. And because we have received mercy, we are called to extend it. People who know they are walking by grace are more gentle with others who are still learning. Today, walk in the truth that you are a new creation. Receive peace and mercy from God, and let them overflow to those around you.
question: How can the peace and mercy you receive from God overflow to others today?
prayer: Lord, I am a new creation in Christ. Let Your peace and mercy rest on me, and help me be gentle and merciful with others who are still learning. Amen.

text: That he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.
reflection: Peter calls believers to a new way of using their time: "That he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God." Notice the phrase the rest of his time. Whatever has happened in the past, the remaining days of our lives can be given to God. That is a hopeful word. It is never too late to begin living for Him. There is also rest in this verse. Living for our own desires is exhausting. Chasing approval, pleasure, and possessions leaves us restless and empty. But living for the will of God brings a deeper peace. When we surrender to His purposes, we stop striving for things that cannot satisfy. Our hearts settle into the place they were made for. Today, consider how you want to spend the rest of your time. Offer your days, hours, and moments to God. Let His will guide your choices. You will find that surrender leads to rest.
question: How do you want to spend the rest of your time, and what would it look like to give it to God?
prayer: Lord, whatever has happened in my past, I give You the rest of my time. Let Your will guide my choices, and let me find rest in surrender. Amen.

text: For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
reflection: God offered His people a surprising strategy for strength: "In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not." They were facing danger and wanted to rush to Egypt for military help. But God said their salvation was in returning to Him and resting in His care. Their strength would come not from frantic activity but from quiet confidence in God. Sadly, they refused. We often respond to pressure the same way. We rush, scramble, and try to fix everything ourselves. But God invites us to return to Him, rest, and trust. Quietness is not passivity. It is the calm of a heart that knows God is in control. Confidence is not arrogance. It is trust in His faithfulness. Today, when you feel the pressure to rush, pause. Return to God. Rest in Him. Find your strength in quiet confidence. Do not be among those who would not.
question: What pressure to rush can you answer today by returning to God in quiet confidence?
prayer: Lord, in returning and rest I am saved; in quietness and confidence is my strength. When I feel pressure to rush, help me pause, return to You, and trust. Amen.

text: To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: Paul greets the believers in Rome with three beautiful descriptions: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace." They were beloved of God. Before anything else, they were loved. They were called to be saints, set apart for God's purposes. And they received grace and peace. Notice the word all. Paul did not single out the most gifted or prominent believers. Every believer in Rome, whether rich or poor, Jew or Gentile, enslaved or free, was beloved and called. This is true of you too. You are beloved of God. That is your identity, the foundation of everything else. And love received becomes love expressed. When we know we are beloved, we can love others freely, without fear or competition. Today, rest in the truth that God loves you. Then let that love shape how you treat the people around you. Treat them as the beloved of God, because they are.
question: How might treating others as the beloved of God change one of your interactions today?
prayer: Father, thank You that I am beloved and called to be a saint. Let Your love free me from competition, and help me treat others as Your beloved too. Amen.

text: And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith…
reflection: Paul was concerned about the young believers in Thessalonica who were facing hardship. So he sent Timothy, "our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith." Timothy's mission was twofold: to strengthen them and to comfort them. Faith can be shaken by trials. When life gets hard, we may wonder if God is still there or if our trust is misplaced. In those moments, we need people who will come alongside us, reminding us of truth and encouraging our hearts. Timothy was that kind of friend. He brought stability and comfort. God still sends people like Timothy. Perhaps someone has encouraged your faith during a difficult season. Thank God for them. And perhaps you are being called to be a Timothy for someone else. Today, reach out to someone whose faith is being tested. Encourage them, pray with them, and help them stand firm.
question: Whose faith is being tested that you could encourage and pray with today?
prayer: Lord, thank You for those who have strengthened my faith in hard times. Make me a Timothy to someone today, to establish and comfort them in their faith. Amen.

text: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.
reflection: Peter writes about the coming day of the Lord, when God will make all things new. Then he draws a practical conclusion: "Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless." Our hope for the future shapes how we live today. Because we look forward to God's new creation, we seek to live in peace and purity now. Notice that Peter calls his readers beloved. This is not a threat but a loving encouragement. And the goal is to be found in peace: at peace with God, at peace within, and at peace with others. That kind of peace requires diligence. It means resolving conflicts, seeking forgiveness, and choosing kindness. It means letting go of grudges. Today, ask yourself whether there is any relationship where peace is missing. Take a step toward reconciliation. Live today as one who is looking forward to that beautiful day.
question: Is there a relationship where peace is missing, and what step toward reconciliation could you take?
prayer: Lord, as I look forward to Your new creation, help me live in peace and purity now. Give me courage to take a step toward reconciliation today. Amen.

text: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
reflection: David wrote this psalm during a time of trouble, perhaps while people were questioning and opposing him. Yet he ends with this peaceful declaration: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety." David did not wait for every problem to be solved before he could sleep. He chose to lie down in peace because he trusted God's protection. Sleep is an act of trust. When we sleep, we are completely vulnerable. We cannot guard ourselves or fix anything. We must let go. David could do that because he knew that God alone kept him safe. Many people struggle with restless nights, lying awake with worries. This verse is a gift for those moments. Before you sleep tonight, pray these words. Hand over your worries to God. Remind yourself that He is awake when you are not. He watches over you. You can lie down in peace, because the LORD makes you dwell in safety.
question: What worries can you hand to God tonight so that you can lie down in peace?
prayer: Lord, You alone make me dwell in safety. I hand You my worries tonight, knowing You are awake when I sleep. I will lay me down in peace. Amen.

text: Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul.
reflection: This proverb speaks to parents and anyone who guides young people: "Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul." Loving correction is not harsh punishment. It is the patient guidance that helps a child walk in the light, learn right from wrong, and grow in wisdom. It takes effort and courage. It is often easier to look the other way. But Proverbs promises that loving discipline bears good fruit. A child who is guided well brings peace and delight to a parent's heart. This principle reflects how God treats us. He corrects us because He loves us. His discipline is not rejection but care. It leads us into the light and gives our souls rest. Today, if you are raising or mentoring young people, ask God for wisdom and patience to guide them lovingly. And when God corrects you, receive it as a sign of His love. His correction leads to rest and delight.
question: Whom are you called to guide with loving correction, and how do you receive God's correction?
prayer: Lord, give me wisdom and patience to guide the young people in my care with love. When You correct me, help me receive it as a sign of Your love. Amen.

text: Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord…
reflection: Hebrews gives a clear instruction: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord." The word follow means to pursue, to chase after. Peace does not happen by accident. It must be pursued, especially in relationships where there is tension. And it must be pursued with all people, not just those we like. Notice that peace and holiness are paired together. Peace without holiness might mean compromising what is right just to avoid conflict. Holiness without peace might mean being right but harsh. God calls us to both: to live in a way that honors Him while doing everything we can to live at peace with others. This is not always easy. Some people may not want peace. But our responsibility is to pursue it from our side. Today, think of a relationship that needs peace. Take one step toward it. And ask God to help you grow in holiness, reflecting His character in all you do.
question: Which relationship needs you to pursue peace, and how can you take one step toward it?
prayer: Lord, help me follow peace with all people, and holiness too. Show me one step I can take toward peace, and grow Your character in me. Amen.

text: And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held…
reflection: John sees a moving scene in heaven: "I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held." These were people who had given their lives for their faith. On earth, they were persecuted and killed. But in heaven, they are safe, near the altar of God. In the following verses, they are given white robes and told to rest a little longer. This vision brings renewal to weary souls. It reminds us that faithfulness is never forgotten. Every sacrifice made for Christ is seen by God. Those who suffer for Him are held close and honored. It also reminds us that our brothers and sisters around the world still suffer for their faith today. We can remember them in prayer. Today, take courage from this picture of heaven. Whatever it costs you to follow Jesus, it is worth it. Your soul is safe in His keeping. Pray for those who are persecuted, and stay faithful.
question: What is following Jesus costing you, and how can you pray for those who are persecuted?
prayer: Lord, my soul is safe in Your keeping. Give me courage to stay faithful whatever it costs, and comfort and strengthen those who suffer for Your name. Amen.

text: Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
reflection: James offers a picture of spiritual renewal: "Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls." First, we lay aside what harms us, the attitudes, habits, and words that pollute our hearts. Then we receive God's Word with meekness, with a humble and teachable spirit. James calls it the engrafted word, like a branch grafted into a tree. When God's Word is planted deep in us, it grows and becomes part of who we are. It renews us from the inside out. This is how renewal happens. Not merely by trying harder, but by clearing away what crowds out God and making room for His Word to take root. Today, consider what you need to set aside. Perhaps it is bitterness, gossip, or an unhealthy habit. Lay it down. Then receive God's Word humbly. Read a passage slowly, and let it be planted deep in your soul.
question: What do you need to lay aside so that God's Word can be planted deep in your soul?
prayer: Lord, help me lay aside what pollutes my heart, the bitterness, the careless words, the unhealthy habits. Plant Your Word deep within me, and let it bear fruit. Amen.

text: Then said Jesus to them again, Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
reflection: On the evening of the resurrection, the disciples were hiding behind locked doors, afraid. Then Jesus appeared among them and said, "Peace be unto you: as my Father hath sent me, even so send I you." His first word was peace. Not rebuke for their failures, not disappointment over their fear, but peace. He calmed their hearts with His presence. And then He gave them a mission. Just as the Father had sent Him, He was sending them. Peace and purpose go together. Jesus does not give us peace so that we can hide comfortably forever. He gives us peace so that we can go out into the world with courage. As this month of peace, rest, and renewal ends, receive His peace afresh. Let it settle your fears. Then hear His sending. You are sent into your family, your workplace, and your community, carrying His peace. Go with confidence. The risen Christ goes with you.
question: Where is the risen Jesus sending you today, carrying His peace?
prayer: Risen Lord, You speak peace to my fears and send me as the Father sent You. Settle my heart with Your peace, and send me out into my family, work, and community. Amen.
